attribution.note: Marcus's own prediction in his 2025 predictions post, listed under 'High confidence'.

semantics.note: An unhedged 'will' under a high-confidence heading, with an end-of-2025 horizon. The proposition keeps 'much of the world' and 'increasingly'.

contract.note: Reading 'look to Europe for guidance' as modelling or advancing EU-style AI rules is an ordinary reading. 'Much of the world' has no threshold and 'increasingly' has no baseline, so the interpretation affects the result.

evidence.note: 2025 CEPA study: few countries copying the AI Act, and the UK, Japan, Australia, Singapore and others taking lighter approaches. Dated April 2025, so it does not cover the whole year.
Vietnam's December 2025 AI law is broadly similar to the EU AI Act. This is one country, so it gives limited support to 'much of the world'.
The EU proposed delaying its own high-risk rules. This bears on how much pull the EU model has, but does not directly measure other countries' choices.

reviews.rationale: The horizon has passed. The best 2025 evidence (e1) matches the contract's contradiction condition: few countries copying the EU, and most major economies choosing lighter, non-EU approaches. Vietnam (e2) and Peru are isolated exceptions and do not amount to 'much of the world'. The EU's proposed delay (e3) fits waning pull. The packet has no systematic count, but the weight of the evidence is against the forecast.

attribution.note: Marcus's own statement reviewing his earlier prediction against 2024.

semantics.note: A retrospective observation that LLMs did not markedly improve Alexa-like assistants during 2024. The scope is kept.

contract.note: The plain reading (no shipped LLM upgrade that made assistants markedly better, with Alexa as the named case) is fair. Which assistants count as 'like Alexa' is left to interpretation.

evidence.note: The planned October 2024 launch of the generative-AI Alexa did not happen; release slipped into 2025.
Same article: Amazon's AI lead gives hallucinations as a reason for the delay. This explains the delay rather than adding outcome evidence.
Gemini Live, an LLM replacement for Google Assistant, rolled out in 2024. The source does not judge it markedly better, so it does not meet the contradiction condition.

reviews.rationale: The named case holds: Amazon did not ship its LLM-powered Alexa in 2024 (e1). The strongest counterpoint, Gemini Live (e3), shipped, but nothing in the packet shows it was widely judged markedly better, which the contradiction condition requires. On the contract's plain reading the claim is supported. Apple's Siri changes were not assessed.

attribution.note: Marcus's own prediction, listed under 'High confidence' in his 2025 predictions post.

semantics.note: An unhedged 'will' with an end-of-2025 horizon. 'Should they arise' is fairly read as describing the scope of the authority, not as a condition on the forecast.

contract.note: Focusing on the US and UK institutes, and counting them under their new names, is an ordinary reading. Any reasonable reading gives the same result.

evidence.note: After its June 2025 rename, the US institute (now CAISI) continues to focus on guidance, testing and evaluation.
CAISI works through voluntary agreements with developers, not binding powers.
Explainer published in 2026, before the evaluation date. It states that neither the US nor the UK institute can legally block a release and that their agreements are voluntary.
A 2025 UK petition asking for AISI to be given blocking powers implies it lacked them. It is a citizen petition, so context only.

reviews.rationale: The horizon has passed. Through 2025 the US and UK institutes kept issuing guidance and running evaluations (e1, e2) under voluntary agreements, and neither had legal authority to block a model's release (e3). The packet has no evidence that any institute gained binding powers. Other countries' institutes were not checked.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assessment in his review of 2024.

semantics.note: An observation about the state of models at the end of 2024. The o3 caveat is kept. The proposition drops the period, but the contract supplies calendar 2024.

contract.note: Splitting the claim into two parts and counting the released o1 is fair, since the caveat names only o3. Whether o1's reasoning gains are 'incremental' turns on interpretation.

evidence.note: Altman said in October 2024 that nothing OpenAI was then working on merited the GPT-5 name. This supports part (b).
o1 rose to 74% on AIME 2024 against GPT-4o's 12%. This is a company disclosure, but the AI Index (e4) independently reports the same jump.
OpenAI's own description of o1. Self-assessment, so context only.
The quoted line shows leading models converging with each other, not that they were at GPT-4 level. The same page reports o1's dramatic reasoning gains.

reviews.rationale: Part (b) holds: OpenAI did not consider anything in 2024 worthy of the GPT-5 name (e1). Part (a) is contradicted on an ordinary reading: o1, released in 2024 and outside the o3-only caveat, made large reasoning gains over GPT-4o (e2, corroborated by the AI Index). The convergence of leading models on chat rankings (e4) partly fits 'surrounded by' similar models.
